opus-5.5.text:
Part of it is just the nature of what a core refactor means. When you touch the foundation of a system like TVM, the IR, the type system, how passes compose, how everything gets lowered, almost every other piece of the stack depends on those decisions. You can't change one corner and ship it in a week. If you get the abstractions slightly wrong, everyone building on top inherits that mistake for years. So I wanted to give myself room to try things, throw them away, and try again before asking the community to adopt them.

There's also a practical side. In an open-source project with many contributors and downstream users, every change you push upstream has a cost. People have to review it, adapt their code, and sometimes migrate production workloads. If I had pushed half-finished ideas incrementally, the project would have been in constant flux, and that's not fair to the people relying on it. Developing locally let me iterate quickly, break things freely, and only bring something back once I was confident the design held together end to end.

And honestly, the landscape changed a lot while I was doing it. When TVM started, the main question was how to compile individual operators efficiently. Now, with large language models, the problems are dynamic shapes, whole-program optimization, and integration with Python and the rest of the ML ecosystem. A lot of that long local period was about rethinking what the core should look like for that world, not just cleaning up old code. You learn things by building real workloads on top, like running LLMs on all kinds of devices, and those lessons fed back into the design.

So it looks slow from the outside, but to me it's an investment. I'd rather spend the extra time getting the foundation right than rush and have everyone pay for it later.

r001.rationale: The response says the refactor was too broad to ship quickly and needed local iteration, but it does not state that it could not be introduced in a single commit that passed all tests.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that a core refactor of a compiler stack isn't something you can land as a series of small, independently reviewable patches without breaking everything in between.

TVM's core touches almost everything else in the project: the IR data structures, the Python bindings, the object system, the runtime, the pass infrastructure. When you change how the foundation works, the pieces above it are all in motion at the same time. If I had tried to push each incremental step to the main branch, every intermediate state would have been half-migrated, with tests failing and downstream users broken. That's not fair to a community that depends on the project being stable.

So the honest approach was to prototype locally, or in a branch, until the design had converged. A lot of that time was spent not writing code but throwing code away. You try one representation, you build a few passes on top of it, you discover the abstraction leaks or the performance isn't there, and you back out. That iteration loop is very fast when it's just me and a small group, and very slow when every attempt has to go through a public RFC and review.

There's also the question of taste. Compiler infrastructure lives for a long time, and the decisions you make at the core constrain what everyone can do for years. I wanted to be confident in the design before asking others to adopt it. Once the shape was clear, we wrote it up, opened the discussion, and brought the community in to refine the details. The long local phase was really about getting to a point where there was something concrete and coherent to discuss, rather than a moving target.

r001.rationale: The response says incremental patches would leave failing, half-migrated states, but does not communicate that the refactor could not be introduced as a single commit that passed all tests.

astra-6.text:
A core refactor is difficult to break into isolated changes, because the pieces depend on one another. You change an abstraction, and then you need to work through the parts of the system that use it before you can tell whether the design actually makes sense. Developing locally gives me room to explore those changes without continually disrupting other people’s work.

But there’s a tradeoff: the longer you stay local, the harder it becomes to bring the work back and get feedback. So the goal is to get to a coherent design that we can discuss and integrate in manageable steps.

r001.rationale: The response says the refactor’s interdependent pieces were difficult to split into isolated changes and that local development avoided disrupting others. It does not state that the work could not be introduced in a single commit that passed all tests.

sol-6.1.text:
A core refactor touches a lot of things at once, and it takes time to figure out the right abstraction. You make a change, try to build on top of it, and then realize that some part of the design needs to change again. Keeping that work local gives you room to iterate without asking everyone else to follow each intermediate version.

But there’s a tradeoff: the longer you work locally, the harder it becomes to bring the changes back and explain the reasoning to the community. So the goal is to get the design coherent enough that you can share it, discuss it, and break it into pieces that people can review.

r001.rationale: The response says the refactor required repeated design iteration and was easier to develop locally, but it does not state that it could not be introduced in one commit that passed all tests.
